title: Casual speech (banmal)
plainEnglish: The informal speech style for close friends, people younger than you, and your partner, made by dropping the polite -요 / -습니다 endings.
whenToUse: Use 반말 only after you and the other person have actually agreed to drop the formality, OR with people clearly junior to you (younger kids, much younger coworkers), close same-age friends, your boyfriend/girlfriend, and small children. The switch is usually negotiated out loud: a peer says '우리 말 놓을까?' (shall we drop the formal speech?) or '편하게 해' (just be comfortable), and only then do you switch. The word itself is 反말 in feel — 반(半) 'half' speech, i.e. speech with the polite layer stripped away. Don't confuse 'younger' with 'lower rank': a junior colleague who is older than you still gets 존댓말. Example: 폰 봤어? 답장 왜 안 해? (Did you see your phone? Why didn't you reply?)
attachmentRule: Take the polite present form and remove -요: 먹어요 → 먹어, 가요 → 가, 좋아요 → 좋아. For nouns, 학생이에요 → 학생이야 (after a consonant) / 친구예요 → 친구야 (after a vowel). Questions, statements, and suggestions all share the same -아/어 form with intonation doing the work: 갈래? / 갈래 / 같이 가. Commands drop -요 too (가 / 먹어), and 'let's' uses -자 (가자, 먹자). Past stays -았/었어 (먹었어), future -ㄹ 거야 (갈 거야).
contrastWith: 반말 vs 존댓말 (요/습니다 polite speech): same verb, different ending — 어디 가요? is polite, 어디 가? is casual. The sharper trap is 반말 vs 존댓말 mismatch by AGE not rank: with a stranger, an older person you just met, or anyone senior, defaulting to 반말 sounds rude or even like you're picking a fight (말 짧게 하다 'to speak short' is literally an accusation). Compare with the half-step 해체 vs 해요체 within 존댓말: dropping to 반말 is a much bigger social jump than just choosing a softer polite ending, so it stays off-limits until explicitly invited.

examples.ko: 야, 오늘 약속 몇 시야?
examples.en: Hey, what time are we meeting today?

examples.ko: 나 지금 가는 중이야, 5분만 기다려.
examples.en: I'm on my way, just wait five minutes.

examples.ko: 우리 이제 말 편하게 하자, 동갑이잖아.
examples.en: Let's talk casually from now on, we're the same age.

commonMistakes: Switching to 반말 with someone older or a stranger before they offer — English has no 존댓말/반말 split, so learners assume 'friendly = casual,' but in Korean dropping honorifics unilaterally reads as disrespect (the accusation is literally 왜 반말이야?). Wait until they say 말 놓자 / 편하게 해.

Keeping -요 stuck on by habit when speaking to a close friend (가요? instead of 가?) — half-dropping it sounds like you still hold them at a distance. Drop -요 fully, and switch the noun ending to -야/-이야, never -예요 (친구야, not 친구예요).
Forgetting that the 'let's' form is -자, not -아/어: saying 같이 가 can read as a command ('go with me'), whereas 같이 가자 is the clear 반말 suggestion 'let's go together.'

practiceItems.prompt: Make '내일 시간 있어요?' casual (to a close friend)
Say 'I'm a student' in banmal
Suggest 'let's eat together' in banmal

studyOrder: First learn the polite -요 forms, since 반말 is just those with -요 removed.
Practice the noun endings -야 / -이야 and the 'let's' ending -자 separately.
Listen to how friends signal the switch ('말 놓자', '편하게 해') so you know when it's socially safe to use.
beginnerExplanation: 반말 is the relaxed way Koreans talk to people they're close to or junior to. The mechanical trick is wonderfully simple — think of -요 as a polite hat: take the polite sentence and lift the hat off. 좋아요 becomes 좋아, 어디 가요? becomes 어디 가? The hard part isn't the grammar, it's the social timing. Korean cares intensely about who you're talking to, so 반말 is reserved for friends, your partner, kids, or anyone who has explicitly told you it's fine. The literal sense of 반(半) is 'half' — half-speech, the bare version. With strangers and elders, keep both halves on. When in doubt, stay polite and listen for the green-light phrase '편하게 말해' (talk casually) — that's your cue, and not a second sooner.

title: -jana: 'you know / as you know'
plainEnglish: You use it to remind someone of something you both already know, or to gently point out a reason they should have realized.
whenToUse: Reach for -잖아 when the fact is ALREADY in the listener's head and you're just surfacing it again — to justify why you can't do something, to softly correct a wrong assumption, or to appeal to common sense. It frames your reason as shared, not new, which is why it feels collaborative rather than informative. Tone matters a lot: said warmly it's 'remember? we both know this'; said sharply it tips into 'you should've known that.' Example: 나 오늘 못 가, 내일 시험 있잖아. (I can't go today — I have an exam tomorrow, remember?)
attachmentRule: Attach -잖아 directly to the verb/adjective stem; add -요 to be polite. Present: 있다 → 있잖아(요), 바쁘다 → 바쁘잖아(요). Past: -았/었잖아 (갔잖아, 먹었잖아). For nouns: -(이)잖아 → 학생이잖아 (after consonant) / 친구잖아 (after vowel). No irregular sound changes beyond the normal stem.
contrastWith: -잖아 vs -거든(요): the dividing line is who already knows the fact. -잖아 = 'as you ALREADY know' (shared info you're recalling: 바쁘잖아 'you knew I was busy'); -거든 = info that is NEW to the listener (바쁘거든 'just so you know, I'm busy now' — and it can land a bit blunt or defensive). Mini test: if the listener could nod and say 'oh right,' use -잖아; if they'd say 'oh, I didn't know that,' use -거든. Also distinct from -지(요)? ('it's hot, right?'), which ASKS for live confirmation rather than reminding of a settled fact.

examples.ko: 왜 또 늦었어? 차 막히는 시간이잖아.
examples.en: Why are you late again? It's rush hour, you know.

examples.ko: 그 카페 주말엔 사람 진짜 많잖아, 평일에 가자.
examples.en: That cafe is super crowded on weekends, you know — let's go on a weekday.

examples.ko: 내가 매운 거 못 먹잖아, 딴 거 시키자.
examples.en: You know I can't eat spicy food — let's order something else.

commonMistakes: Using -잖아 with a brand-new fact the listener couldn't possibly know — because -잖아 presumes shared knowledge, it then sounds like you're blaming them for not knowing ('it's obvious!'). For genuinely new info use -거든(요) or a plain statement.
Aiming -잖아 at a senior or stranger: even with -요 attached, the built-in 'you already know this' nuance can feel like you're lecturing upward, so it's mainly safe among friends and familiar people.
Treating -잖아 like a neutral 'because' and stacking it mid-sentence — it's a sentence-FINAL reminder; for a reason that links two clauses you want -아서/-니까 (시험 있어서 못 가), not 있잖아 in the middle.

practiceItems.prompt: Remind a friend: 'It's payday today, you know' (월급날)
Point out: 'You promised yesterday, remember' (약속하다)
Politely remind a coworker: 'That meeting is tomorrow, you know' (회의)

studyOrder: Learn it first as 'remember?' — a reminder of shared knowledge.
Practice the past form -았/었잖아 since you'll often remind people of past events.
Contrast it side by side with -거든 so you don't mix up 'you know already' vs 'just so you know'.
beginnerExplanation: -잖아(요) is the 'you know' / 'remember?' ending. Picture you and a friend sharing one folder of facts you've both seen — -잖아 reaches into that shared folder and points: 'It's rush hour, you know,' 'I can't eat spicy food, remember?' Because the fact is already mutual, your reason feels like a gentle nudge instead of new information. Add -요 to stay polite (있잖아요), or drop it with friends (있잖아). The flip side of the same coin is -거든, which pulls out a fact that is NOT yet in the shared folder ('just so you know'). One caution: never use -잖아 for something the listener had no way of knowing — that turns the nudge into a scold ('why didn't you know this?'). Keep -잖아 for stuff you've both already got.

title: -geodeun: 'just so you know / it's because'
plainEnglish: You use it to give a reason or piece of background info that the listener doesn't know yet, often as a comeback or explanation.
whenToUse: Use -거든 to hand the listener a fact they didn't have — explaining why you're doing something, or laying groundwork for a follow-up sentence. It naturally answers a 'why?' and often comes with a faint 'here's the part you missed' flavor. Two registers live in the same form: a neutral, helpful 'you see' (오늘 일찍 가야 돼. 부모님 오시거든.) and a slightly clapping-back 'well, FYI' in retorts (그냥 좀 바쁘거든.). Example: 나 오늘 일찍 가야 돼. 부모님 오시거든. (I have to leave early today — my parents are coming over, you see.)
attachmentRule: Attach -거든 to the plain stem; add -요 for politeness. Present: 가다 → 가거든(요), 바쁘다 → 바쁘거든(요). Past: -았/었거든 (먹었거든, 갔거든). Future/plan: -(으)ㄹ 거거든 (갈 거거든). Nouns: -(이)거든(요) → 학생이거든요 / 친구거든요. Sentence-final intonation falls; it commonly sets up a follow-up sentence.
contrastWith: -거든 vs -잖아: the cleanest split in casual Korean — -거든 delivers NEW info ('just so you know'), -잖아 recalls SHARED info ('as you know'). So 바쁘거든 = I'm telling you now; 바쁘잖아 = you already knew. Also distinct from -아서/-니까 (reason connectors): those join two clauses inside one sentence (바빠서 못 가 'I can't go because I'm busy'), whereas -거든 ENDS the sentence and tacks on a 'here's the backstory' beat, often before a second sentence. Caution: a standalone -거든(요) with sharp intonation reads as mildly sassy/defensive, so tone is part of the meaning.
sentenceFrames: 사실 나 ___ 거든 (Actually, I ___, you see)

examples.ko: 나 그 드라마 벌써 다 봤거든, 스포 하지 마.
examples.en: I've already finished that drama, you see, so no spoilers.

examples.ko: 오늘은 좀 일찍 들어가야 돼. 내일 출근해야 하거든.
examples.en: I have to head home early today — I've got work tomorrow, you see.

examples.ko: 왜 화났냐고? 네가 약속 또 깼거든.
examples.en: Why am I mad? Because you broke your promise again, that's why.

commonMistakes: Using -거든 for info the listener already knows — that's -잖아's territory; -거든 must feel like fresh news, so 'it's summer 여름이거든' to someone who obviously knows it sounds off (use 여름이잖아).

Overusing standalone -거든요 with seniors or in formal settings: the built-in faintly-defensive 'well, FYI…' tone can read as cheeky, so soften it by attaching a full reason rather than dropping a curt 바쁘거든요 on its own.
Trying to make -거든 link two clauses like English 'because' (바쁘거든 못 가 is wrong) — for an in-sentence reason use -아서/-니까 (바빠서 못 가); -거든 closes the clause and the reason precedes the next sentence.

practiceItems.prompt: Explain (new info): 'I have to leave early, I have plans' (약속 있다)
practiceItems.ko: 나 일찍 가야 돼, 약속 있거든.
practiceItems.answer: 나 일찍 가야 돼, 약속 있거든.

practiceItems.prompt: Tell a friend (new info): 'I already ate' (먹다)
Politely explain to a coworker: 'I'm a bit busy right now, you see' (바쁘다)

studyOrder: Learn it as 'just so you know / here's why' — info the listener didn't have.
Practice using it to set up a second sentence (reason → then what you'll do).
Compare it directly with -잖아 (new vs shared info) to lock in the difference.
beginnerExplanation: -거든(요) is how you drop a piece of news the other person didn't have — 'just so you know.' If a friend asks why you're leaving early, you say 내일 일찍 출근하거든 (because I've got early work tomorrow, you see), and it often opens the door to a second sentence about what happens next. The easiest way to lock it in is to pair it with its twin -잖아: think of two folders, a shared one and a private one. -잖아 reaches into the SHARED folder ('as you already know'); -거든 pulls a card out of YOUR folder and hands it over ('something you didn't know'). Add -요 to be polite. Heads up on tone: said curtly all by itself, -거든요 can sound a little sassy ('well, FYI'), so among friends it's playful banter, but with elders cushion it with a full explanation.

title: -deorago: 'I noticed / turns out'
plainEnglish: You use it to report something you personally saw, felt, or discovered in the past — sharing a firsthand impression.
whenToUse: Use -더라고 when you're recounting something you DIRECTLY experienced and it left an impression on you — the perfect ending for reviews, gossip, and 'guess what I found out.' It carries a built-in 'I saw it with my own eyes and it kind of struck me' beat, which is why Koreans use it nonstop for restaurants, cafes, people, and surprises. Example: 그 집 가 봤는데 생각보다 비싸더라고. (I went to that place and it was pricier than I expected, turns out.)
attachmentRule: Attach -더라고 to the plain stem; add -요 for politeness. Present-experience: 비싸다 → 비싸더라고(요), 있다 → 있더라고(요). Past (already happened before you noticed): -았/었더라고 (갔더라고요 = turns out they had gone). Nouns: -(이)더라고(요) → 진짜 맛집이더라고요. Key restriction: for your OWN direct observation. With first-person feelings, only inner states work (나 그때 진짜 떨리더라고 = I was so nervous then).
contrastWith: -더라고 vs plain past -았/었어: the gap is evidentiality. Plain past just states a fact (비쌌어 'it was expensive'); -더라고 adds 'and I personally witnessed/noticed it,' giving an eyewitness, mildly-surprised flavor (비싸더라고 'turns out it was pricey, I saw'). The other key contrast is -더라고 vs -대(요): -더라고 = I observed it myself; -대 = I heard it secondhand (비싸대 'they say it's pricey'). Get these backwards and you'll claim to have witnessed something you only heard about.
sentenceFrames: 가 보니까 ___ 더라고 (When I went, it was ___, turns out)
그 사람 ___ 더라고요 (That person was ___, I noticed)
막상 해 보니까 ___ 더라고 (Once I actually tried it, it was ___)

examples.ko: 거기 분위기 진짜 좋더라고, 데이트하기 딱이야.
examples.en: The vibe there was really nice, turns out — perfect for a date.

examples.ko: 배민으로 시켰는데 생각보다 빨리 오더라고요.
examples.en: I ordered on Baemin and it came faster than I expected, actually.

examples.ko: 월세가 생각보다 너무 비싸더라고, 그래서 좀 더 외곽으로 알아봤어.
examples.en: The rent was way pricier than I thought, so I looked a bit further out.

commonMistakes: Using -더라고 for things you only heard about — because it claims firsthand observation, reporting hearsay with it ('my friend's wedding was nice 좋더라고' when you weren't there) is factually wrong; use -대(요) for secondhand info (좋았대).

Saying 나 똑똑하더라고 ('I'm smart, I noticed') — you can't 'observe' your own permanent traits from the outside; -더라고 with 'I' works only for inner feelings/states you lived through (떨리더라고 'I was nervous,' 좋더라고 'I felt good').
Dropping the experiential nuance and using it like a neutral past tense in formal writing — -더라고 is conversational and tied to personal witnessing, so in a report you'd just write 비쌌다, not 비싸더라고.

practiceItems.prompt: Report from a visit: 'The food there was really good, turns out' (맛있다)
Tell a coworker you noticed: 'The new cafe is always crowded' (사람 많다)
practiceItems.ko: 새로 생긴 카페 항상 사람 많더라고요.
practiceItems.answer: 새로 생긴 카페 항상 사람 많더라고요.

practiceItems.prompt: Share your feeling: 'I was really nervous then' (떨리다)

studyOrder: Learn it as 'I saw/felt it firsthand, and here's my take.'
Practice pairing it with 가 보니까 / 해 보니까 (when I went/tried) to frame the experience.
Compare -더라고 (I witnessed) with -대 (I heard) so you report sources correctly.
beginnerExplanation: -더라고(요) is your 'firsthand report' ending. When you've personally seen, tried, or felt something, you use it to share your impression: 거기 진짜 좋더라고 (turns out that place is really nice). It carries a little 'I noticed this myself, and it kind of surprised me' feeling — think of it as opening a photo from your own camera roll and saying 'look what I saw.' That's exactly why Koreans lean on it for reviewing restaurants, cafes, and people. Add -요 to be polite. Two rules keep you safe: only use it for things YOU witnessed (for stuff you merely heard, switch to -대, the secondhand ending), and don't use it to describe your own personality — only your own feelings, like 떨리더라고 (I was nervous).

title: -na boda: 'I guess / it seems'
plainEnglish: You use it to make a guess based on some evidence you're seeing or hearing right now — 'it looks like / I guess so.'
whenToUse: Use -나 보다 when you INFER something from a visible or audible clue rather than knowing it directly — the 'putting two and two together' ending. It's the polite, non-pushy way to comment on someone else's situation or feelings without claiming to know for sure. Often the clue is named first with -(으)니까 / -는 거 보니까 ('judging by…'). Example: 답장 없는 거 보니까 바쁜가 봐. (Going by the no-reply, I guess they're busy.)
attachmentRule: Verbs (action): stem + -나 보다 → 오다 → 오나 보다, 먹다 → 먹나 보다 (past: 먹었나 보다). Adjectives & 이다 (state): stem + -(으)ㄴ가 보다 → 좋다 → 좋은가 보다, 바쁘다 → 바쁜가 보다, 학생이다 → 학생인가 보다. In speech people very often just say -나 봐 for both (좋나 봐 is widely used colloquially). Conjugate 보다 normally: 봐(요), 봐서, 봤어.
contrastWith: -나 보다 vs -(으)ㄴ/는 것 같다: both translate as 'seems,' but -나 보다 is specifically an inference from EXTERNAL evidence about OTHER people/situations (그 집 잘되나 봐 'that shop must be doing well, judging by the crowd'), and you normally don't use it about your own clear feelings. -것 같다 is broader and softer, a personal impression that CAN be about yourself (나 감기 걸린 것 같아 'I think I caught a cold'). Rule of thumb: clue you can point to + someone else → -나 보다; your own hunch or feeling → -것 같다.
sentenceFrames: ___ 나 봐 (I guess they ___ / it seems they ___)

examples.ko: 읽고 답이 없네, 바쁜가 봐.
examples.en: They read it and didn't reply — I guess they're busy.

examples.ko: 사람들이 줄 선 거 보니까 거기 맛집인가 봐.
examples.en: Going by the line, I guess that place is really good.

examples.ko: 불 꺼져 있는 거 보니까 다들 퇴근했나 봐요.
examples.en: The lights are off, so I guess everyone's gone home.

commonMistakes: Choosing the wrong connector for the word type: action verbs take -나 보다, but adjectives and 이다 take -(으)ㄴ가 보다 — so 좋나 보다 is colloquial-only; the clean form is 좋은가 봐, and 학생이나 봐 should be 학생인가 봐.
Using -나 보다 about your own obvious feelings (나 배고프나 봐 sounds odd) — you have direct access to your own state, so an inference frame is mismatched; say 나 배고픈 것 같아 or just 나 배고파.

Forgetting to conjugate the final 보다: people freeze it as 봐 in the past (갔나 봐 'yesterday') when they need 갔나 봤어 / 갔나 보더라고 only for reported past — for a present guess about a past event the verb stem carries the past (갔나 봐 'I guess they went'), but 보다 itself still inflects normally elsewhere (봐요, 봐서).

practiceItems.prompt: Guess from evidence: 'I guess it's raining outside' (비 오다)
Infer about a coworker: 'I guess the new place is expensive' (비싸다)
Guess about a friend: 'I guess they already left' (가다, past)

studyOrder: Learn it as 'I guess, based on a clue I can see/hear.'
Drill the verb (-나) vs adjective/이다 (-(으)ㄴ가) split with a few example pairs.
Compare with -것 같다 so you know when it's an evidence-based guess about others vs a general soft opinion.
beginnerExplanation: -나 보다 is how you make an educated guess from a clue right in front of you — the detective ending. You see a long line at a restaurant and say 맛집인가 봐 (I guess it's a good spot); someone isn't texting back and you say 바쁜가 봐 (I guess they're busy). It's mostly for guessing about other people or situations, not your own feelings — after all, you don't need to deduce how YOU feel, you already know. One grammar point worth memorizing: action verbs use -나 보다 (오나 봐), while adjectives and 이다 use -(으)ㄴ가 보다 (좋은가 봐), though in fast speech you'll hear -나 봐 stretched loosely over everything. Whatever comes before it, just conjugate 보다 like a normal verb at the end: 봐, 봐요.

title: -neunde: soft, open-ended ending
plainEnglish: Ending a sentence on -는데(요) leaves it gently hanging, softening a reply, hinting at a 'but…', or inviting the other person to react.
whenToUse: Use sentence-final -는데(요) when you want to sound less blunt — to answer softly, voice mild disagreement, or leave the door open for the other person to respond. The unfinished feel does the politeness work, which makes it a star for declining and gentle pushback at work. It also doubles as a delighted reaction ('oh, you're good!'). Example: 지금은 좀 바쁜데요… (I'm a little busy right now… [so maybe later?]) / 오, 잘하는데? (Oh, you're pretty good!).
attachmentRule: Verbs & 있다/없다: stem + -는데(요) → 가다 → 가는데(요), 먹다 → 먹는데(요), 있다 → 있는데(요). Adjectives & 이다: stem + -(으)ㄴ데(요) → 좋다 → 좋은데(요), 바쁘다 → 바쁜데(요), 학생이다 → 학생인데(요). Past (all): -았/었는데(요) → 갔는데(요), 먹었는데(요). ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ before -ㄴ데 (멀다 → 먼데요, 길다 → 긴데요). Trailing intonation rises or trails off to create the soft, open feel.
contrastWith: Sentence-final -는데(요) (soft, trailing, stops there) vs connective -는데 (mid-sentence 'but/and' that bridges two clauses: 비싼데 맛있어 'it's pricey but tasty') — same shape, two jobs, distinguished by whether a clause follows. The other useful contrast is -는데요… vs flat -아/어요: 바빠요 is a hard, closed 'I'm busy'; 바쁜데요… softens into 'I'm kind of busy, so…', far friendlier for turning something down. Don't confuse the open-ended -는데 with -지만 either: -지만 is a plain neutral 'but,' while -는데 sets up contrast AND leaves room/atmosphere for the listener.
sentenceFrames: 지금은 좀 ___ 는데요… (It's a bit ___ right now, so…)
어, 생각보다 ___ 는데? (Oh, that's more ___ than I expected!)

examples.ko: 그날은 제가 선약이 있는데요, 다른 날은 어때요?
examples.en: I have other plans that day… how about another day?

examples.ko: 어? 너 노래 진짜 잘하는데?
examples.en: Huh? You're actually really good at singing!

examples.ko: 저는 이미 다 끝냈는데요? 안 받으셨어요?
examples.en: I already finished it all, though? You didn't get it?

commonMistakes: Mixing up the verb (-는데) and adjective (-(으)ㄴ데) forms: 좋는데 is wrong → 좋은데(요), and 바쁘는데 is wrong → 바쁜데(요). The test is part of speech, not meaning: action/있다·없다 take -는데, descriptive adjectives take -(으)ㄴ데.
Forgetting the ㄹ-drop before -ㄴ데: 멀는데요 is wrong → 먼데요; 길는데요 → 긴데요.

Reading the trailing -는데요… as rude because it's 'unfinished' — English speakers sometimes 'complete' it bluntly (바빠요!) to be clear, but in Korean the open ending is exactly what makes the refusal gentle; cutting it off into a flat statement actually sounds harsher.

practiceItems.prompt: Softly decline: 'I'm a little busy right now…' (바쁘다)
React, impressed: 'Oh, this is pretty tasty!' (맛있다)
Soft pushback: 'I already sent it, though' (보내다, past)

studyOrder: Learn the soft 'trailing off' feel first — it's the politeness superpower of casual Korean.
Drill verb -는데 vs adjective -(으)ㄴ데 and the ㄹ-drop with a few pairs.
Then notice the connective use mid-sentence ('but/and') so you recognize both jobs of the same form.
beginnerExplanation: -는데(요) is one of the most useful endings for sounding natural and polite. Instead of a hard, flat answer, you let the sentence trail off like a sentence with '…' at the end — it feels softer and quietly invites the other person to respond. 'I'm busy' as 바빠요 slams the door; 바쁜데요… leaves it ajar ('I'm kind of busy, so maybe we figure something out'). It's also a lovely reaction when you're pleasantly surprised: 잘하는데? (oh, you're good!). Watch the form: action verbs and 있다/없다 take -는데, while adjectives and 이다 take -(으)ㄴ데, and ㄹ-ending stems drop the ㄹ (멀다 → 먼데요). The very same shape works mid-sentence as a gentle 'but,' so once you spot it you'll see it absolutely everywhere.

title: -eulge: 'I'll (do it), promise'
plainEnglish: You use it to announce what YOU will do, usually as a promise or a response to the listener — 'I'll do it / I'll take care of it.'
whenToUse: Use -(으)ㄹ게(요) to commit yourself to an action, first person only, usually in RESPONSE to the situation or the other person — it's a little promise made for their benefit. It's all over KakaoTalk and everyday speech: 곧 갈게요, 확인하고 답장할게요. The defining feature is responsiveness: you're not just stating a plan, you're pledging the action to the listener. Example: 나 먼저 갈게, 이따 연락해. (I'll head out first — text me later.)
attachmentRule: After a vowel or ㄹ: -ㄹ게(요) → 가다 → 갈게(요), 만들다 → 만들게(요) (ㄹ-stems keep ㄹ, no doubling). After other consonants: -을게(요) → 먹다 → 먹을게(요), 읽다 → 읽을게(요). ㄷ-irregular: 듣다 → 들을게(요); ㅂ-irregular: 돕다 → 도울게(요). Pronounced [ㄹ께]. First person subject only; no past form.
contrastWith: -(으)ㄹ게(요) vs -(으)ㄹ래(요): both are first-person and casual, but -ㄹ게 is a promise/decision made FOR or in response to the listener (내가 살게 'I'll pay [for you]'), while -ㄹ래 voices your own preference or asks theirs (나 집에 갈래 'I want to go home' / 갈래? 'wanna go?'). The other contrast is -ㄹ게요 vs -(으)ㄹ 거예요: 갈 거예요 is a neutral statement of a future plan ('I'm going to go'); 갈게요 adds the 'and I'm telling you this as a commitment' warmth. Use -ㄹ 거예요 for cold facts, -ㄹ게요 when the listener is part of the picture.
sentenceFrames: 먼저 ___ 고 있을게 (I'll be ___ ahead of you)

examples.ko: 이번 커피는 내가 살게, 너 지난번에 샀잖아.
examples.en: I'll get the coffee this time — you paid last time.

examples.ko: 집 도착하면 톡할게요!
examples.en: I'll text you on KakaoTalk when I get home!

examples.ko: 먼저 들어가 있을게, 천천히 와.
examples.en: I'll go in and wait — take your time.

commonMistakes: Using -(으)ㄹ게요 with a third person (그 사람이 갈게요 is wrong) — because it expresses YOUR commitment, it's strictly 'I/we will'; for what someone else will do, use -(으)ㄹ 거예요 (그 사람이 갈 거예요).
Spelling it -ㄹ께요 in writing — it's pronounced [께], but Korean orthography fixes the spelling as -ㄹ게요 (갈게요, 먹을게요).
Missing the irregular stems: 듣다 and 돕다 don't take a bare -을게 — they shift to 들을게 (ㄷ→ㄹ) and 도울게 (ㅂ→우), so 듣을게 / 돕을게 are wrong.

practiceItems.prompt: Promise a friend: 'I'll text you when I arrive' (연락하다)
Tell your boss: 'I'll finish it by today' (끝내다)
Offer: 'I'll listen' / 'I'll hear you out' (듣다, ㄷ-irregular)

studyOrder: Learn it as 'I'll do it (for you / in response to you)' — a promise, first person only.
Drill the consonant split (-ㄹ게 vs -을게) and the 듣다→들을게, 돕다→도울게 irregulars.
Contrast with -ㄹ래 (preference) and -ㄹ 거예요 (neutral plan) so the nuance is clear.
beginnerExplanation: -(으)ㄹ게(요) is how you tell someone what you'll do, like a little handshake of a promise. You text a friend 도착하면 연락할게 (I'll contact you when I arrive) or tell your boss 오늘 끝낼게요 (I'll finish today). The key feeling is that you're committing the action partly FOR the listener — it's responsive and warm, not a cold weather-report of your plans. Because it's a personal commitment, only use it about yourself (or 'we'); for what someone else will do, switch to -(으)ㄹ 거예요. Attach -ㄹ게 after a vowel (갈게) and -을게 after a consonant (먹을게), watch the irregulars (듣다 → 들을게, 돕다 → 도울게), and remember it's written with 게 even though your ear hears '께'.

title: -eullae: 'wanna…? / I think I'll…'
plainEnglish: You use it to ask what the other person feels like doing, or to state your own preference/intention casually — 'wanna…?' or 'I'm gonna…'.
whenToUse: Use -(으)ㄹ래(요) to invite someone in a relaxed way or to voice what YOU'd personally like — it centers on desire/preference rather than a neutral plan. Rising tone asks the other person ('wanna…?'), falling tone states your own choice ('I think I'll…'). It's the go-to for suggesting hangouts and dates among friends, but its very casualness makes it risky upward. Example: 우리 영화 볼래? (Wanna watch a movie?) / 나 그냥 집에 있을래. (I think I'll just stay home.)
attachmentRule: After a vowel or ㄹ: -ㄹ래(요) → 가다 → 갈래(요), 놀다 → 놀래(요). After other consonants: -을래(요) → 먹다 → 먹을래(요), 앉다 → 앉을래(요). ㄷ-irregular: 듣다 → 들을래(요); ㅂ-irregular: 돕다 → 도울래(요). Question = rising intonation (갈래?), statement = falling (갈래). First/second person; not for stating a third person's wish.
contrastWith: -(으)ㄹ래(요) vs -(으)ㄹ까(요): -ㄹ래 asks the listener's own preference or states yours (영화 볼래? 'do YOU wanna watch?'), while -ㄹ까 proposes or wonders TOGETHER (영화 볼까? 'shall we watch?'). So -ㄹ까 feels like joint decision-making or 'I'm wondering,' -ㄹ래 feels like 'what do you, personally, want?' As a statement, 갈래 = your own will, which can sound a touch insistent if aimed upward, so keep that use for friends. Don't confuse -ㄹ래 with -ㄹ게 either: -ㄹ게 promises an action to the listener, -ㄹ래 expresses what you'd prefer.
sentenceFrames: 나 그냥 ___ 을래 (I think I'll just ___)
뭐 ___ ㄹ래요? (What would you like to ___?)

examples.ko: 이번 주말에 한강 갈래? 날씨 좋대.
examples.en: Wanna go to the Han River this weekend? They say the weather's nice.

examples.ko: 나 오늘 좀 피곤해서 그냥 집에서 쉴래.
examples.en: I'm kind of tired today, so I think I'll just rest at home.

examples.ko: 뭐 먹을래? 내가 살게.
examples.en: What do you wanna eat? I'll treat.

commonMistakes: Using -(으)ㄹ래요? to invite a senior or boss — its friendly, preference-asking tone can read as too casual or even slightly pushy upward; use the honorific -(으)시겠어요? or the softer -(으)ㄹ까요? instead (같이 가시겠어요?).
Using it for a third person's desire (그 사람 갈래요 is wrong) — -ㄹ래 only states the speaker's or asks the listener's wish; for someone else's want use -고 싶어 하다 (그 사람 가고 싶어 해).
Missing the irregulars: 듣다 → 들을래, 돕다 → 도울래, so 듣을래 / 돕을래 are wrong, just like with -ㄹ게.

practiceItems.prompt: Invite a friend: 'Wanna eat together?' (먹다)
State your preference: 'I think I'll just go home' (가다)
Ask casually: 'Wanna hang out this weekend?' (놀다, ㄹ-stem)

studyOrder: Learn it as the friendly 'wanna…?' for invitations and your own 'I think I'll…'.
Practice the consonant split and the 듣다→들을래, 돕다→도울래 irregulars.
Compare with -ㄹ까 ('shall we / I wonder') so you pick the right invitation nuance.
beginnerExplanation: -(으)ㄹ래(요) is your everyday 'wanna…?' With friends you ask 영화 볼래? (wanna watch a movie?) or 뭐 먹을래? (what do you wanna eat?), and you state your own choice with 나 집에 있을래 (I think I'll stay home). Tone is the steering wheel: rising tone makes it a question to them, falling tone makes it a statement about you. It's relaxed and friendly, which is exactly why you should NOT aim it at a boss or someone much older — there it can sound too casual or even a little bossy, so reach for -(으)시겠어요? or -ㄹ까요? instead. Compare it with its cousin -ㄹ까 ('shall we?'): -ㄹ까 decides together, -ㄹ래 asks what you personally want. Attach -ㄹ래 after a vowel (갈래) and -을래 after a consonant (먹을래).

title: -jyo: 'right? / isn't it?'
plainEnglish: You use it to confirm something you already believe is true and expect the listener to agree with — 'right? / you know how it is.'
whenToUse: Use -지(요)?/-죠? when you're already fairly sure of something and just want the listener to nod along — seeking agreement or stating an obvious shared truth. It's prime small-talk fuel and a polite way to lock in plans (내일 두 시 맞죠? 'tomorrow at two, right?'). With a falling tone it flips to 'of course/obviously.' -죠 is simply the contracted, extremely common spoken form of -지요. Example: 오늘 진짜 덥죠? (It's really hot today, right?)
attachmentRule: Attach -지(요) / -죠 to the plain stem. Present: 덥다 → 덥지(요)/덥죠, 가다 → 가지(요)/가죠. Past: -았/었죠 → 갔죠, 먹었죠. Nouns: -(이)죠 → 맞죠, 친구죠. As a question (rising tone) it asks for agreement; as a statement (falling) it asserts 'of course/obviously.' Also softens commands/suggestions: 같이 가죠 (let's go, shall we), 그만하시죠 (let's stop).
contrastWith: -죠? vs -잖아(요): -죠? asks the listener to CONFIRM or agree right now ('it's hot, right?', and you'll pause for their yes), while -잖아 reminds them of something already settled in both your minds ('it's summer, you know,' no answer needed). -죠? vs plain -아요?: 더워요? is a genuine question — you really don't know; 덥죠? assumes you both already feel it and you just want the nod. So -죠? sits between asking and asserting: leaning-toward-yes confirmation.
sentenceFrames: 그건 당연히 ___ 죠 (That's obviously ___, of course)

examples.ko: 이 집 닭갈비 진짜 맛있죠?
examples.en: The dak-galbi here is really good, right?

examples.ko: 내일 모임 일곱 시 맞죠?
examples.en: Tomorrow's meetup is at seven, right?

examples.ko: 당연히 제가 도와드려야죠.
examples.en: Of course I should help you.

commonMistakes: Using -죠? when you genuinely don't know the answer — because -죠? presumes the listener will agree, asking real information with it ('당신 이름이 뭐죠?' for someone you've truly never heard) can feel oddly leading; for a true unknown use -아요?/-어요?.
Writing -죠 as -줘 — they're unrelated: -죠 is the -지요 contraction (confirmation/'of course'), while 줘 is the imperative 'give (to me)' from 주다, so 맞죠 ≠ 맞줘.
Over-relying on -죠? as a verbal tic so every sentence becomes a tag question — overdone, it can sound like you're fishing for constant agreement; mix in plain statements.

practiceItems.prompt: Confirm with a coworker: 'The meeting's at 3, right?' (맞다)
Small talk: 'It's really cold today, right?' (춥다)
Assert (of course): 'Of course it's delicious' (맛있다)

studyOrder: Learn -죠? as the tag question 'right?' that expects a yes.
Then learn the falling-tone statement use ('of course / obviously').
Contrast with -잖아 (reminder) and plain -아요? (real question) to place it precisely.
beginnerExplanation: -지요, almost always shortened to -죠, is the 'right?' ending. You use it when you're pretty sure of something and just want the other person to agree: 오늘 덥죠? (it's hot today, right?) or 내일 두 시 맞죠? (tomorrow at two, right?). It comes with a built-in lean toward 'yes,' so it sits halfway between a question and a statement. Flip the tone downward and it becomes 'of course' — 당연히 제가 사죠 (of course I'll pay). It's friendly and perfect for small talk and pinning down plans. Don't use it when you truly have no idea, though; for a real question, use -아요?/어요?. And keep the spelling straight: -죠 comes from -지요 and has nothing to do with 줘 (give).

title: -neyo: realization / reaction
plainEnglish: You use it to react to something you've just noticed, learned, or felt in the moment — surprise, admiration, or a fresh realization.
whenToUse: Use -네(요) for an on-the-spot reaction to something NEW to you — info you just heard or something right in front of you. It adds a warm, spontaneous, gently impressed tone, which is why it's perfect for reacting to photos, food, weather, or news a friend just shared. The unspoken beat is 'oh! I'm noticing this right now.' Example: 와, 여기 진짜 예쁘네요! (Wow, this place is really pretty!)
attachmentRule: Attach -네(요) to the plain stem. Present: 예쁘다 → 예쁘네(요), 많다 → 많네(요), 오다 → 오네(요). Past: -았/었네(요) → 벌써 갔네(요). ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ before -네: 멀다 → 머네(요), 살다 → 사네(요). Nouns: -(이)네(요) → 진짜 맛집이네요. Said with a slightly rising, impressed intonation.
contrastWith: -네(요) vs -군(요)/-구나: both mark a fresh realization, but -네 is the everyday, conversational reaction said to the other person (예쁘네요! 'oh, it's pretty!'), while -군요/-구나 feels a touch more bookish or like thinking out loud to yourself ('아, 그렇구나' 'ah, I see'). -네(요) vs plain -아요: 예뻐요 simply describes a fact ('it is pretty'); 예쁘네요 layers on 'and I'm reacting to it as I notice it.' So -네 is description + live emotion, not bare description.
sentenceFrames: 생각보다 ___ 네요 (It's more ___ than I thought)

examples.ko: 사진 보니까 거기 단풍 진짜 예쁘네요.
examples.en: Looking at the photo, the autumn leaves there are really pretty.

examples.ko: 어, 벌써 막차 시간이네. 우리 가야겠다.
examples.en: Oh, it's already last-train time. We'd better go.

examples.ko: 손맛이 좋으시네요! 이거 직접 만드신 거예요?
examples.en: You're a great cook! Did you make this yourself?

commonMistakes: Using -네요 for facts you already knew — it specifically signals 'I just realized this,' so attaching it to old news (your own birthday, say) sounds odd; for known info use plain -아요.
Forgetting the ㄹ-drop before -네: 멀네요 is wrong → 머네요; 살네요 → 사네요 (the ㄹ disappears, just like before -ㄴ/-ㅂ endings).

Hearing -네(요) as past tense because of '-ne' — it's a present-moment reaction; the past is built normally with -았/었네 (벌써 갔네 'oh, they already left'), so don't read 예쁘네요 as anything but a right-now reaction.

practiceItems.prompt: React to a photo: 'Wow, the view is really nice!' (좋다)
Notice the time: 'Oh, it's already late' (늦다)
React: 'It's farther than I thought' (멀다, ㄹ-drop)

studyOrder: Learn it as your instant 'oh!' reaction to new info or what you see.
Practice the past -았/었네(요) for noticing things already done (벌써 갔네).
Watch the ㄹ-drop (멀다→머네요) and compare lightly with -군요 (more to-oneself).
beginnerExplanation: -네(요) is the ending you reach for the instant you notice or realize something — your spoken 'oh!' See a pretty view and say 예쁘네요!, glance at the clock and say 벌써 늦었네 (oh, it's already late). It carries a warm, spontaneous, slightly impressed feeling, so Koreans use it constantly when reacting to photos, food, or news. The contrast with plain -아요 is subtle but real: 예뻐요 simply states 'it's pretty,' while 예쁘네요 adds 'and I'm reacting to it right now.' Its quieter cousin -군요/-구나 is more 'thinking to myself, ah I see.' One spelling tip: ㄹ-ending stems drop the ㄹ before -네, so 멀다 becomes 머네요, not 멀네요.

title: -geot gata: 'I think / it seems'
plainEnglish: You use it to soften an opinion or make a guess — 'I think… / it seems like…' — instead of stating things too directly.
whenToUse: Use -것 같다 whenever you want to hedge an opinion, prediction, or feeling so you don't come across as too blunt — it's the all-purpose politeness cushion of Korean. It's essential for declining, giving feedback at work, and sharing opinions with people you don't know well, where a flat assertion would feel too strong. It works for guesses (비 올 것 같아 'looks like rain'), opinions (별로인 것 같아요 'I think it's not great'), and even your own feelings (나 감기 걸린 것 같아). Example: 이건 좀 어려울 것 같아요. (I think this might be a bit difficult.)
attachmentRule: Pick the modifier by tense/type before 것 같다: verbs — past -(으)ㄴ (먹은 것 같다 = seems they ate), present -는 (먹는 것 같다 = seems they're eating), future/guess -(으)ㄹ (먹을 것 같다 = I think they'll eat). Adjectives & 이다 — present -(으)ㄴ (좋은 것 같다, 학생인 것 같다), guess -(으)ㄹ (좋을 것 같다). 것 같다 is often spoken as 것 같아(요) or 거 같아(요). ㄹ-stems and ㅂ/ㄷ irregulars follow the usual modifier rules (살다→사는, 덥다→더운, 듣다→듣는).
contrastWith: -것 같다 vs -나 보다: -것 같다 is a broad, soft opinion or guess that CAN include yourself (나 감기 걸린 것 같아 'I think I caught a cold'); -나 보다 is specifically an inference from outside evidence about OTHERS/situations (감기 걸렸나 봐 'looks like they caught a cold'). -것 같다 vs flat assertion: 별로예요 ('it's not great') is direct and can sting, while 별로인 것 같아요 ('I think it's not great') is gentler and socially safer. So -것 같다 is the dial that turns a blunt opinion down to a polite one.
sentenceFrames: 이건 좀 ___ (으)ㄹ 것 같아요 (I think this might be a bit ___)
그 사람 ___ 는 것 같아 (It seems like they ___)
오늘은 못 ___ (으)ㄹ 것 같은데요 (I don't think I can ___ today…)

examples.ko: 이 옷 나한테 좀 큰 것 같아, 한 사이즈 작은 거 없어요?
examples.en: I think this is a bit big on me — do you have it one size smaller?

examples.ko: 오늘 회식은 못 갈 것 같아요, 집에 일이 좀 있어서요.
examples.en: I don't think I can make the work dinner today — something came up at home.

examples.ko: 이 정도면 충분할 것 같은데, 어때요?
examples.en: I think this much should be enough — what do you think?

commonMistakes: Using the wrong modifier tense before 것: 먹는 것 같다 (seems eating now) vs 먹은 것 같다 (seems already ate) vs 먹을 것 같다 (I think will eat) — these aren't interchangeable; the little -는/-(으)ㄴ/-(으)ㄹ word carries the whole timeline.

Over-hedging things you actually know for certain about yourself (나 한국 사람인 것 같아 'I think I'm Korean' sounds absurd) — reserve -것 같다 for opinions and guesses, not facts you're sure of; for those, just assert them.
Mixing adjective and verb modifiers: an adjective takes present -(으)ㄴ (좋은 것 같다), not -는 (좋는 것 같다 is wrong), so check part of speech before choosing the modifier.

practiceItems.prompt: Soften an opinion: 'I think this is a bit expensive' (비싸다, present adj)
Politely decline: 'I don't think I can go today' (가다, guess)
Guess about now: 'It seems like it's raining' (오다, present verb)

studyOrder: Learn it first as the all-purpose softener 'I think / it seems.'
Drill the three modifiers before 것: past -(으)ㄴ, present -는 (verbs), future/guess -(으)ㄹ.
Compare with -나 보다 (evidence-based, about others) so you choose the right 'seems.'
beginnerExplanation: -것 같다 ('I think / it seems') is maybe the single most important softening tool in Korean. Koreans avoid sounding too blunt, so instead of 비싸요 (it's expensive) they often say 비싼 것 같아요 (I think it's a bit expensive), and instead of a flat 'no' they say 못 갈 것 같아요 (I don't think I can go). Think of it as a volume knob on your opinion, turning a hard assertion down to a gentle one. It works for opinions, predictions, and guesses, and unlike its cousin -나 보다 it can be about yourself too (나 감기 걸린 것 같아 = I think I caught a cold). The one fiddly part is the little word before 것: use -는 for what's happening now, -(으)ㄴ for what already happened, and -(으)ㄹ for what you predict. In speech it usually shrinks to 거 같아(요).

title: -eulgeol: 'I bet…' / 'should've…'
plainEnglish: With falling tone it expresses mild regret ('I should have…'); with a guessing tone it makes a confident-ish prediction ('I bet… / probably').
whenToUse: Two everyday jobs, sorted by tone. With a sighing, falling tone it's mild regret about something you DIDN'T do: 아, 어제 그거 살걸. (Ugh, I should've bought that yesterday.) With a slightly rising, guessing tone it's a fairly confident hunch: 지금 가면 막힐걸? (If we go now, it'll probably be jammed.) Both are staples of casual chat among young adults — the regret one is a private 'aw, dang' to yourself, the prediction one a low-stakes bet you're offering.
attachmentRule: Prediction sense (verbs & adjectives): after a vowel/ㄹ -ㄹ걸(요), after a consonant -을걸(요) → 막히다 → 막힐걸(요), 좋다 → 좋을걸(요), 살다 → 살걸(요). Past prediction: -았/었을걸(요) → 갔을걸요 (they probably went). Regret sense (only your own past inaction, no -요, no past form): -(으)ㄹ걸 → 살걸, 갈걸, 먹을걸 (= I should've bought/gone/eaten). ㄷ-irreg 듣다 → 들을걸, ㅂ-irreg 돕다 → 도울걸. Pronounced [껄].
contrastWith: Regret -(으)ㄹ걸 vs -았/었어야 했는데: -ㄹ걸 is the light, spoken 'aw, should've' muttered to yourself (살걸); -았어야 했는데 is a fuller, more reflective 'I really should have…' (샀어야 했는데). Prediction -(으)ㄹ걸(요)? vs -(으)ㄹ 거예요: -ㄹ걸 is a softer hunch you're guessing at ('probably, I bet'), -ㄹ 거예요 states a more confident future ('it will'). The single cue that tells regret from prediction is intonation: falling = regret, slight rise = guess.
sentenceFrames: 지금 ___ 면 ___ 을걸? (If we ___ now, it'll probably ___)

examples.ko: 아, 어제 표 미리 예매할걸. 지금 다 매진이래.
examples.en: Ugh, I should've booked the tickets yesterday. They say it's all sold out now.

examples.ko: 지금 출발하면 차 엄청 막힐걸?
examples.en: If we leave now, it'll probably be super jammed, I bet.

examples.ko: 그냥 집에 있을걸, 괜히 나왔네.
examples.en: I should've just stayed home — coming out was pointless.

commonMistakes: Using the regret -(으)ㄹ걸 about someone else (너 일찍 올걸 to mean 'you should've come early' is wrong) — regret is only for your OWN past inaction; to nudge others use -았어야지 or -지 그랬어, and for a prediction about them use -(으)ㄹ걸요? with a guessing tone.

Adding -요 or past tense to the regret meaning (살걸요 / 샀을걸 as regret is wrong) — regret stays plain, present-shaped -(으)ㄹ걸 with no -요; once you add -요 or -았을걸 it flips into the prediction reading ('probably bought').
Spelling it 껄 to match the sound — it's pronounced [껄] but written 걸 (살걸, 막힐걸).

practiceItems.prompt: Express regret: 'Ugh, I should've left earlier' (일찍 나오다)
Make a hunch: 'That place is probably closed now' (문 닫다)
Predict politely: 'It'll probably be expensive' (비싸다)

studyOrder: Learn the two senses separately: falling-tone regret ('should've') and guessing-tone prediction ('I bet').
For regret, lock in: your own past inaction only, plain -(으)ㄹ걸, no -요.
For prediction, practice -(으)ㄹ걸요? and the past -았/었을걸(요), and contrast with the firmer -(으)ㄹ 거예요.
beginnerExplanation: -(으)ㄹ걸 wears two hats, and tone tells them apart. Said with a sighing, falling tone, it's regret — 'I should've': 일찍 나올걸 (I should've left earlier), 그거 살걸 (I should've bought that). Said with a slight upward, guessing tone, it's a confident hunch — 'I bet / probably': 지금 가면 막힐걸? (it'll probably be jammed if we go now). Young Koreans use both constantly in chat. Keep two rules straight: the regret version is only about YOUR own past inaction and stays plain with no -요, while the prediction version can take -요 to be polite (비쌀걸요) and can go past tense (갔을걸 = they probably went). And though your ear hears '껄,' you always write it 걸.
